Amazon Athena

Source: vignettes/athena.Rmd
athena.Rmd

Amazon Athena runs SQL queries over data in Amazon S3 and other configured sources. oauth_db_athena() opens a DBI connection using the visitor’s JWT access token through IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation. AWS applies the data permissions configured for that identity.

This requires an administrator to connect your identity provider to AWS. An ordinary AWS console login or an AWS access key isn’t that integration.

Prepare the workgroup and sign-in

Install odbc in R and the Amazon Athena ODBC 2.x driver, version 2.5.0.0 or later, on the Shiny server. The driver is available for Windows, macOS and Linux x86_64. You don’t need an AWS SDK for R or Python.

Ask your AWS administrator to follow Connect Athena to IAM Identity Center. The deployment needs a trusted external token issuer, a federated IAM application role, an access role and an Identity Center customer managed application associated with the Athena workgroup. Configure user matching and the users’ Lake Formation/data permissions too. Signing in doesn’t create those grants.

Register a Web OAuth app with your identity provider, with http://localhost:8100 as the redirect URI. It must issue JWT access tokens whose issuer and audience AWS accepts. Ask the administrator for the delegated scopes to request; there is no universal Athena scope. AWS also needs to be able to reach the issuer’s signing keys.

Save the settings in a local .Renviron, then restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_ATHENA_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting
OAUTHDB_ATHENA_SCOPES=database.read
OAUTHDB_ATHENA_WORKGROUP_ARN=arn:aws:athena:eu-west-1:123456789012:workgroup/reporting
OAUTHDB_ATHENA_APPLICATION_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AthenaApplication
OAUTHDB_ATHENA_OUTPUT=s3://your-query-results/reporting/
Setting Where to get it
Issuer, client ID, secret and scopes Your identity provider’s OAuth registration and the administrator who configured AWS trust
Workgroup ARN Athena console, under the configured workgroup; includes its region and name
Application role ARN The IAM application role configured for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
S3 output location The results bucket/prefix approved for this workgroup

The application role and access role serve different purposes. Supply the application role to application_role_arn; the driver uses the deployment’s tags to discover the other role and Identity Center application. Workgroup settings can override the supplied results location or encryption settings. Follow your organization’s rules for access to saved query results.

A complete app

Save this as example.R. Replace the query’s table name with one that your users can read. Signing in runs the query, and Athena may charge for it.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

athena_scopes <- strsplit(
  Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ATHENA_SCOPES"), " ", fixed = TRUE
)[[1L]]

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ATHENA_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "offline_access", athena_scopes)
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_athena(
    auth$connection,
    workgroup_arn = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ATHENA_WORKGROUP_ARN"),
    application_role_arn = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ATHENA_APPLICATION_ROLE_ARN"),
    s3_output_location = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ATHENA_OUTPUT"),
    required_scopes = athena_scopes,
    schema = "default"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT * FROM example_table LIMIT 20")
  })
}

runApp(shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"), port = 8100, launch.browser = FALSE)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100

If your provider needs a resource/audience parameter, configure that on the shinyOAuth client according to your provider’s requirements. For Microsoft Entra, use oauth_db_microsoft_client() with a custom token target for your registered resource, then select it with target on oauth_db_athena(). The Redshift guide shows this client configuration pattern; use your Athena integration’s resource and scopes.

Driver settings

workgroup_arn supplies both AwsRegion and Workgroup, so those settings can’t point to different workgroups. Set catalog and schema to select the data catalog and database. Set driver if your installed driver’s registered name differs from "Amazon Athena ODBC Driver".

For a deployment without ARN-discovery tags, supply access_role_arn and customer_idc_application_arn explicitly. Both must belong to the same AWS partition as the workgroup; their accounts can differ.

The helper accepts these options through ...:

  • R odbc options: timeout, timezone, timezone_out, bigint, encoding, name_encoding, interruptible.
  • Driver timeouts/polling: ConnectionTimeout, RequestTimeout, MaxPollDuration, MinQueryExecutionPollingInterval, MaxQueryExecutionPollingInterval, QueryExecutionPollingIntervalMultiplier.
  • Results/metadata: RowsToFetchPerBlock, ResultFetcher, StringColumnLength, ComplexTypeColumnLength, BinaryColumnLength, S3ResultBlockSize, UseWCharForStringTypes, UseSingleCatalogAndSchema, QueryExternalCatalogs.
  • Results encryption and CA configuration: S3OutputEncOption, S3OutputEncKMSKey, TrustedCerts.

See AWS’s main connection parameters and advanced options for their values and units. TrustedCerts follows the driver’s platform rules: Windows uses its system trust store. TLS verification stays enabled. The default result fetcher can use S3 or streaming; check the driver’s network and permission requirements, including port 444 for streaming.

DSNs, AWS keys/profiles, alternate authentication, endpoint overrides and native logging options aren’t accepted. The helper supplies JWT_TIP, the visitor token and a random role session name, and disables file credential caching, connection-check caching and result reuse. It doesn’t write the token to a file or replace the Shiny process’s AWS credentials.

Connections and renewal

Call con() before each operation. The helper reuses a valid connection while its token is unchanged. A changed token replaces the connection on the next access; finish reading and clear outstanding DBI results first. Ordinary token renewal doesn’t rerun completed reactive queries. Sign-out, account changes, permission loss and session end close the connection.

Identity Center may restrict repeated exchanges of tokens containing a jti claim. A reconnect can therefore require a newly issued access token; if the provider can’t renew it, sign in again. The helper doesn’t enable a shared credential cache or replay a failed query to work around this.

Closing the connection doesn’t guarantee that AWS cancels a submitted query. Use Athena’s query history and your workgroup’s limits to manage running queries and costs. Clear app-cached results on account changes as described in Getting started.

Validation boundary

Offline tests cover driver arguments, credential isolation, token renewal, connection cleanup, rejected overrides and construction of this app. The native Linux fixture checks token forwarding and TLS hostname rejection, then opens connections and runs SQL using synthetic AWS protocol responses. It checks separate users and renewed tokens with interleaved queries. These checks don’t establish live Identity Center exchange, Lake Formation grants, S3 result access or query execution. Validate those with two differently authorized users in your configured AWS deployment before relying on it.
